newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya Cen Bank intervenes to stem shilling fall.
newsitem.headline: Kenya Cen Bank intervenes to stem shilling fall.

text.p: The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday to stem the shilling fall on continued jitters after political unrest early in the week, Governor Micah Cheserem said.
Cheserem said the shilling rate versus the dollar had eased to as low as 61.50 for bids from around 55 at the beginning of the week.
The central bank offered $19 million to the market and there were few takers, he told Reuters.
The CBK posted opening rates for the day at 57.61 against the dollar compared to 56.38 on Thursday. Against the pound, the shilling was posted at a commercial mean of 97.27 from 95.10.
Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since a violent campaign in July 1990 that helped persuade Moi to allow multi-party politics.
The violent protests have upset investors and made many wary of this emerging market. Turnover on the Nairobi stock exchange has slumped to a year's low.

Commercial bank dealers posted rates in the 59-61 range and maintained spreads as wide as three shillings. Signals from the central bank that it had more dollars than market demand was expected to calm market nerves and see shilling gains.
The shilling was poised to recoup some losses, they said.
"There has been overeaction in the market," Cheserem said, adding that quoted rates for the shilling were ridiculous.
The shilling last touched the 60 range and threatened further losses versus the dollar in October 1993.
Bank dealers said Thursday's move from 56.30 to a close as low as 59.30 against the dollar had sent waves of panic in the market, which they thought was an overreaction.
"Central bank has been in the market this morning and we do not have any takers," a treasurer from a top bank said.
Cheserem, 47, who is one of Kenya's leading economic reform leaders, said one bank asked for $5 million but took only $1 million when the bank said it would meet the demand.
Another official at the central bank said state utility Kenya Power & Lighting Corp asked for $6.5 million but then backed down after the bank also said it would meet the demand.
Cheserem said the market would calm as both sides of Kenya's political divide settled their differences. "The biggest word in town is dialogue. Dialogue in block letters."
Earlier in the week, commercial dealers said the market had become so nervous that they feared the shilling would not be able to recoup its losses without central bank intervention.
